## 8. Models

<!-- models:start (generated by tools/process_models.mjs; edit outside these markers) -->

### Cross-stitch (`lumenary:cross-stitch`, models this process)

_From: Counted thread embroidery; when: Centuries old, charted patterns from the 19th century; works best on: Bold, simple subjects with distinct colours._

Cross-stitch is counting: the cloth is a grid of holes, and every stitch fills exactly one square. That makes the whole craft a pixel art problem. Shrink the picture to one pixel per square, limit the colours to a box of flosses and draw an X in each square, with back threads below and front threads on top for a woven look.

**How it is made, as the model does it:**

1. Shrink the picture to one pixel per square of cloth.
2. Find the k most representative colours with k-means, made slightly more saturated, and give each square the nearest.
3. Optionally leave squares lighter than 0.86 bare.
4. Draw the cloth with faint threads along every grid line and a dark hole at every corner.
5. Draw each stitch as two strokes: back strokes first in a slightly darker shade, then a soft shadow, then the front strokes with a thin pale highlight for the twist.

**The maths:**

$$s=\frac{W}{n},\qquad \text{inset}=0.15\,s,\qquad \text{thread width}=0.34\,s$$

_Geometry of a stitch for n stitches across._ (primitives: stitch-grid)

$$c(i,j)=\arg\min_{f\in F}\ \big\lVert \bar P_{ij}-f\big\rVert_{\text{redmean}}$$

_Each square takes the floss in the set F nearest to the average colour of its pixels; redmean is a distance that weights red and blue by brightness._ (primitives: coarse-grid, palette-snap)

**Dials:** `across` (Stitches across) = 68 [30 to 140]; `flosses` (Colours of thread) = 8 [3 to 14]; `cloth` (Cloth) = "cream" (cream, white, black, blue); `bare` (Leave light areas bare) = false; `seed` (Different flosses) = 1.

**History:** Counted thread embroidery has been worked for many centuries. Samplers, in which girls recorded stitches, alphabets and mottoes, were made from the sixteenth century onward, and printed charts of the nineteenth century, such as Berlin wool work, spread patterns widely. Today cross-stitch is a hobby for people who enjoy slow, careful making.
